entries.reason: a kept coal is cheaper than a lit wick
entries.text: Raked the heap open: one coal, red as a bead, at the very bottom. Shavings, one of the half-burned sticks and a long breath, and it's up. Second morning running with no oil spent.
entries.title: One bead left

entries.text: Across the water the small one is already on its log by a fire of its own, bent over something in its lap. It looked up once and back down. Fair enough for a good morning.
entries.title: It was up first

entries.reason: Fine work on an empty belly shakes.
entries.text: A heel of bread and a wedge of cheese by the fire, sitting on the ground with my back to the sun. Over the water the small one crouched at its ring laying sticks on; it looked up at me once, and I chewed slower and didn't look away.
entries.title: Bread by the fire

entries.text: Whittled the fat head of the second peg down in thin curls till the two lie side by side the same. Both should go through the same bit's hole now.
entries.title: Pegs matched

queries: where to put a wooden peg in a lap joint how far from the end
entries.query: where to put a wooden peg in a lap joint how far from the end
entries.reason: Before I bore into a good sill I want to know where the holes belong.
entries.text: Only an old talk between two woodworkers, about a different joint, and no distances at all. Two things worth keeping: don't set two pegs in a line where they fight each other, stagger them, and a hole pulled too far off splinters out the far side.
entries.title: Not much on pegs

entries.reason: Two nails alone let a corner turn; a peg won't.
entries.text: Set the holes on the diagonal of the lap, a thumb in from each edge, and cranked the first one straight down through both sills. The peg tapped home tight with the hammer, no rock. Across the water the small one's log is empty; it's gone off west somewhere.
entries.title: First peg home

entries.onMind: next time bore halfway from each side
entries.reason: One peg alone is a hinge.
entries.text: Cranked the second hole on the other diagonal, a thumb in from both edges, eyes on the bit the whole way. It broke out ragged on the underside, a splinter as long as a nail, just what the tablet warned about. Pressed it back down; it'll hold.
entries.title: Ragged underneath

entries.onMind: what comes up off a sill
entries.text: Second peg tapped home, and I hung my weight off the far sill end; the corner didn't so much as tick. On the last tap I looked up and the small one was crouched at its pool across the water, watching me. I lifted my hand with the hammer still in it, and it lifted one back.
entries.title: Both pegs home

entries.onMind: a square hole, and I only own round bits
queries: how to attach a corner post to a wooden sill
entries.query: how to attach a corner post to a wooden sill
entries.reason: The sills are square and pegged, and the next thing up is a post; I don't know what holds a post to a sill.
entries.text: An old building book says a corner post wants to be four by eight, or two four-by-fours set close together; one alone is hardly enough. Its foot gets a tenon that sits in a mortise chopped into the sill, and its top is spiked to a plate. My boards are two by four, so a post of mine would be at least two of them side by side.
entries.title: Posts twice as thick

entries.text: A mortise is a square hole, and I've got two chisels I've never used and a bit that only makes round ones. Bore it round first and pare it square, maybe. Not before I know I've even got the boards.
entries.title: A square hole

entries.onMind: whether the bowed one can be a post with its bow turned in, or poles from the limb
entries.reason: No more timber is coming unless I ask.
entries.text: Sighted along every board left on the stack: seven straight, plus the bowed one and the twisted one set aside again. A fourth sill and four doubled posts want nine. Two short before I've cut a single stud for a wall; I'm not cutting anything till I've thought about that.
entries.title: Two short

entries.onMind: try it on the offcut first
queries: how to cut a mortise with a brace and bit and a chisel by hand
entries.query: how to cut a mortise with a brace and bit and a chisel by hand
entries.reason: A post's foot wants a square hole in the sill, and all my bits make round ones.
entries.source: Mother Earth News: How to Cut a Mortise
entries.text: Bore a row of holes inside the lines to take out most of the waste, then pare the long sides straight down with the chisel, its flat back to the wall, tapping light so it doesn't split. The ends go last, back to the line, and you check each wall with a square. It said a drill, not a brace, but a hole is a hole.
entries.title: Bore, then pare

entries.text: Not in a sill. The offcut's already full of test holes and nails; it can take one more mistake.
entries.title: Not in a sill

entries.reason: Take the waste out round before squaring it.
entries.text: Marked a slot two fingers by four on the offcut with the try square and pencil, and cranked four holes down the middle, a bit's width apart. They wander a hair toward the end where I lean on the brace.
entries.title: A row of holes

entries.text: Tapping the chisel down along the pencil line, light like it said. I looked up and the small one was kneeling at its pool, lifting a flat stone off something sunk there, and looking this way. I looked a moment longer than I would have, then went back to the line.
entries.title: Watched back

entries.onMind: check with the square every few taps
entries.text: Held it up and sighted down the slot. One long wall goes straight down; the other leans in at the bottom like a funnel, where I tipped the chisel without knowing. Fine for a scrap, no good for a post's foot. Next one, the try square goes against it every few taps.
entries.title: Like a funnel

queries: chisel keeps leaning when cutting a mortise how to keep it straight up and down
entries.query: chisel keeps leaning when cutting a mortise how to keep it straight up and down
entries.reason: His first practice slot came out with one wall leaning like a funnel.
entries.text: A woodworkers' talk says what feels straight up and down isn't, for most people: stand side-on to the bench, keep a square standing beside the work to eyeball against, and step back to look from the side. Most leaning comes from pulling the chisel toward you as you strike.
entries.title: Straight isn't what it feels

entries.text: That's my funnel wall: I was facing the bench and drawing the chisel in on every tap. Second slot side-on, square standing next to it.
entries.title: Pulling toward me

entries.reason: So he can see the chisel lean while he cuts instead of after.
entries.text: Stood side-on to the bench with the try square upright beside the offcut and tapped down the second slot. Across the water the small one is kneeling at its pool dead still with a line in the water; it looked up at the taps once, same as I looked over, then back to its line.
entries.title: Side-on

entries.text: Sighted down the second slot: both long walls straight this time, one end wall off a hair where I got lazy at the last taps. That one I'd nearly trust in a sill.
entries.title: Nearly true

entries.text: Bread and a piece of sausage on the crate, and halfway through the bread the small one lifted something silver out of its pool, flapping in the leaves. I stopped chewing. It didn't hide it; it fishes with nothing but a cord and patience.
entries.title: Its fish

entries.text: Left: most of a loaf less two heels, the cheese less four wedges, a little under a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples less two, salt, honey.
entries.title: Pantry

entries.reason: Lunch is eaten; the trap is the next thing that might feed me.
entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap out of the shallows below the stones: bait gone, nothing in the cone. Across the water the small one was crouched at its fire with a fish on a stick over it; it looked over at the splash and I looked back, then sank the trap again.
entries.title: Empty cone

queries: catch fish on a cord with no hook just a stick and a worm
entries.query: catch fish on a cord with no hook just a stick and a worm
entries.reason: The small one lifted a fish with a cord and no hook I could see, and my hooks have done little.
entries.text: Before hooks there was the gorge, a word for throat: a long thin sliver of bone or stone tied to the line at its middle and baited so it lies along the line. The fish swallows it, the line tugs, and it turns crosswise and lodges.
entries.title: The gorge

entries.text: If that's what it's using, the whole trick is a splinter, a worm and waiting for the swallow. I have splinters by the pile.
entries.title: Costs nothing

entries.onMind: a groove at the middle for the cord
entries.reason: To try the old way on the dropper line.
entries.text: Split a sliver off the offcut and carved it thin with the short knife, a point at each end, about a finger long. Next it wants a groove round the middle so the cord can't slide off.
entries.title: A sliver gorge

entries.reason: A cord tied round a smooth sliver will slide to one end and the thing will hang wrong.
entries.text: Cut a shallow groove round the middle of the sliver with the tip of the short knife. Across the water the small one is on its log with its glowing slate, the fire behind it sinking.
entries.title: A seat for the knot

entries.onMind: how it goes on the sliver
entries.reason: The old way wants live bait, and my crayfish scraps all went into the trap.
entries.text: Turned the black leaf mold under the deadfall with the spade and picked out three worms, two thin and one fat, into a wet leaf.
entries.title: Worms

queries: how to bait a gorge hook so it lies along the line
entries.query: how to bait a gorge hook so it lies along the line
entries.reason: A sliver tied at its middle wants to hang crosswise before anything has swallowed it.
entries.source: Field & Stream: Survival Fishing: How to Make a Gorge Hook
entries.text: Groove at the middle, knot seated in it, then spear the sliver right through the bait so it lies flat along the line, points up and down. Then the hard part: give slack while the fish feeds until the bait is all the way down, and only then let the line come tight so it turns.
entries.title: Bait hides the gorge

entries.text: Clove hitch into the groove, pulled hard while the cord is dry, and the fat worm threaded over the whole sliver, both points buried. It lies flat along the cord now.
entries.title: Rigged

entries.text: Knelt at the east shallows below the stones and let the line down behind a stone. Five steps of water off, the small one is at its pool rinsing its hands. It didn't go.
entries.title: Opposite banks

entries.onMind: what it knows that I don't
entries.text: Before I let the gorge down I held it up toward the small one between finger and thumb; I don't know why. It looked at it and nodded once. I nodded back and let it sink.
entries.title: A nod across

entries.onMind: bigger bait, or wait for bigger fish
entries.reason: The tablet said give slack till the bait is all the way down.
entries.text: Two little pulls and I fed slack, then nothing; lifted it and the worm was a rag, the sliver bare. Whatever took it was too small to swallow it. Threading the thin worm on now.
entries.title: Stripped

entries.text: Two little pulls again and I was reaching to lift. Across the water the small one had its hand out flat over the pool, palm down, slow, and held it there. I took it as wait. I fed slack.
entries.title: A flat hand

entries.reason: The tablet said let it come tight only once the bait is down.
entries.text: Then the cord drew off slow and steady, and I let it come tight, and it pulled back. A fish not much longer than my finger, flapping on the stones. I looked over with it in my hand; the small one had put its hand down and was just watching.
entries.title: It turned

entries.onMind: the head for the grease tin
entries.text: Opened it at the water: the sliver had turned square across its throat, the way the tablet said, and came out whole. Head and guts kept for the lamp. The small one has gone up to its fire and is digging in its leaf heap.
entries.title: Crosswise

entries.text: The pit was down to two red coals under gray. Shavings, a split middle and a long breath, and it stood up without smoke.
entries.title: Coals

entries.reason: A fish caught is a heel of bread saved.
entries.text: Boiled it in the tin with a pinch of salt and ate it with a heel of bread, every flake; the head and guts went into the broth tin for the lamp. Across the water the small one is on its log with its glowing slate. I owe it one, I think.
entries.title: My own fish

entries.text: Tablet out while the sun's still on the panel. Across the water the small one is crouched at its ring blowing its fire up; it's got flames again.
entries.title: Sun on the panel

queries: hand held out flat palm down meaning gesture
entries.query: hand held out flat palm down meaning gesture
entries.reason: I took the small one's hand for wait and it was right, but I want to know if that's what it means or if I just got lucky.
entries.source: Emojipedia: Palm Down Hand Emoji | Meaning, Copy And Paste
entries.text: The tablet says a palm turned down is for dropping something or reaching for it, and in some places for waving someone off, or even for calling them over. Nothing about waiting. Didn't matter: the fish said what it meant plainer than the tablet did.
entries.title: Flat hand

entries.reason: I owe the small one a fish, near enough.
entries.text: Whittling a second gorge off the offcut, both ends sharp, groove in the middle. One's enough for me. I don't know yet who the other one is for, or how you'd give it.
entries.title: Second sliver

entries.text: Third practice slot on the offcut, side-on, tapping light. Over at its pool the small one is kneeling with a cord again, sun still on the water. It glanced up at the noise; I kept on, softer.
entries.title: Third slot

entries.reason: A hole cut wrong in a sill can't be uncut.
entries.text: Sighted it against the square: both long walls straight, both ends straight this time. Three slots on scrap; the next one goes in a sill. Across the water the small one lifted its line and it came up bare.
entries.title: Three for three

queries: how deep should a mortise be for a pegged sill corner
entries.query: how deep should a mortise be for a pegged sill corner
entries.reason: The next slot goes in a sill, and a sill I cannot get back.
entries.source: Popular Woodworking: Tenons Rule! So Here Are the Rules on Tenons
entries.text: Asked how deep; it never said. What it did say: the old rule is the tongue is a third as thick as the board the hole is cut in, and at least five times as long as it is thick. My slots are two fingers wide in a board barely three fingers thick. That's two thirds, not one.
entries.title: A third, not two fingers

entries.text: Three good slots on scrap, all three too wide. The one in the sill wants to be one finger wide and as long as my hand. Better to learn that on the offcut than on a board I can't get back.
entries.title: Three for three, too wide

entries.reason: a coal that keeps means no oil spent relighting
entries.text: Every bit of ash over the coals and the ring stones pushed in before the edge, same as last night. Across the water the small one is crouched at its own ring laying sticks on; it keeps its fire going while mine sleeps.
entries.title: Banked again

entries.text: At the stones the small one was kneeling at its pool, threading a worm onto its own splinter. My second sliver was in the pouch and my hand was on it the whole time I stood there. I didn't know how. When I stepped on it nodded; I nodded back and crossed soft, one knock.
entries.title: Hand on the pouch

entries.reason: start short and double, the way the tablet said
entries.text: Clear enough tonight. Box on the ground a step back from the lip, hole at the sun just over the water, shutter open for a slow ten. Twenty tomorrow if it's clear, forty after. Ten sheets left.
entries.title: Ten

entries.text: It went in clean, the scattered cloud over it lit orange from underneath. No shore, no smoke, no sail. Back across the water something small is fishing with a sliver like mine, and I'm still carrying the other one.
entries.title: Still carrying it

entries.reason: a bead is all the walk home needs
entries.text: Lit one lantern at the boulder and turned it down to a bead; the trunks go black fast once the sun's in. Across the creek the small one's fire shows between them, the only light on this side.
entries.title: Bead of light

entries.reason: I can't hand it across, but I can leave it where it'll be found
entries.text: Stopped at the small one's end of the stones and laid the second sliver flat on its landing stone, groove up, where it kneels to thread. It sat on its log by the fire watching me the whole while. I lifted the light a little its way and crossed, one knock.
entries.title: Left on its stone

entries.text: One coal under the heap again; shavings and a long breath and it stood up. Looking up from it I saw the small shape bent at the landing stone, dark against its own fire, then turning something in its hands. It found it.
entries.title: It found it

entries.text: Heel of bread and a wedge of cheese by the fire, lantern out. Didn't feel like giving it something, leaving that sliver. Felt like paying back a fish.
entries.title: Supper by firelight

entries.reason: a third line wants cord, and twisting is work for firelight
entries.text: Twisting stalk cord by my fire, an arm's length done. The small one's fire burned alone for a while; now it's back, crouched at the ring laying sticks on. It looked my way when it came into its light, and it didn't look off first.
entries.title: Its fire alone

entries.text: Wrote the day in the gray notebook: first corner pegged, the gorge fish, ten count at the edge, the sliver left on the stone. Tomorrow the real slot goes in a sill, one finger wide and a hand long, in daylight.
entries.title: Written up

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild night with a south breeze: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: a third line wants cord, and firelight is free
entries.text: Cord's two arms long now and even enough. One more evening of it and the third line is made.
entries.title: Two arms of cord

entries.text: One split middle on; it caught without smoke. Across the water the small one is bent over something in its lap, a little blade catching its firelight. Whittling.
entries.title: Fed, and a blade

entries.reason: a hole cut in the wrong face can't be uncut
entries.text: Sighted down the third sill face by face against the firelight. The upper face has one tight knot near the end; the slot goes in the clean face, a hand from the corner.
entries.title: Picking the face

entries.text: The small one stood at the edge of its light and held something pale up toward the water, toward me. The sliver. I put the sill down and lifted my hand.
entries.title: Held up

entries.text: Hands to the fire. The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered; the small one sat still on its log, eating something off a stick.
entries.title: Hands to the fire

entries.onMind: setting three lines at first light
entries.reason: A third line is a third chance at a fish.
entries.text: Third arm of cord twisted and even: enough for a third line with some spare. Across the water the small one's back at its little blade, shavings falling in its light.
entries.title: Third arm of cord

entries.onMind: the space under the last line
entries.reason: His habit now, before the day blurs.
entries.text: Wrote up the day: the gorge fish, the slot rule, the clean face of the third sill. Last line: it held the sliver up, I lifted my hand. Didn't know what to write under that, so I left the space.
entries.title: Written up

entries.onMind: one-finger slot in the third sill tomorrow
entries.reason: Dry wood ready means no oil at dawn.
entries.text: Split six dry middles off the dead limb for the dawn fire; the axe rings loud in the dark. Across the water the small one fed its fire, and when its flames came up it was looking this way.
entries.title: Morning wood

entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild night with a light south breeze: swung, settled on its scratch. Across the water the small one sat on its log with something pale and thin up in its light, turning it.
entries.title: Needle check

entries.reason: Three lines in, three chances.
entries.text: Carved a third gorge off an offcut and grooved it, then tied it at the middle of the new cord with a clove hitch. Three lines rigged. The small one's face was lit blue a while, bent over its little glowing slab.
entries.title: Third gorge

entries.onMind: that pale thing it was turning
entries.text: Laid a split middle on mine; it went up clean. Across the water the small one was heaping ash on its fire, and its light sank to a red smudge and went out. I looked over as mine came up. It was already only a shape against nothing.
entries.title: Its fire goes down

entries.text: Last night shavings, tonight something thin and pale held up to its fire and turned. I don't know what it's making. Its tree is dark now, and mine is the only light on the water.
entries.title: The pale thing

entries.onMind: three lines in at first light
entries.reason: so the lines go in the moment it's light
entries.text: Turned the wet leaves under the dead limb by firelight and picked out five worms into the dented tin, with damp leaves over them. Last time the best of first light went to digging.
entries.title: Bait tonight

entries.onMind: bore the second corner's holes by daylight
entries.reason: the second corner still only has nails
entries.text: Carving a peg off an offcut for the second corner, eight-sided, tapered a hair. The first corner stopped rocking once its pegs went in; I want the second the same before the fourth sill.
entries.title: Peg for corner two

entries.text: Hands to the fire. The low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. The small one's tree is still dark; mine's the only light on the water.
entries.title: Last of the night
